newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FOCUS - BELGIUM TO GET THIRD GSM NETWORK.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - BELGIUM TO GET THIRD GSM NETWORK.

text.p: The Belgian government is inviting telecoms operators to enter bids for a third GSM mobile telephone network in Belgium, the government said on Friday.

"Within a year from now the government wants to select the operator with a view to have an operational third network within two years," Deputy Prime Minister Elio di Rupo said after the weekly cabinet meeting.
He also said the government was inviting bids for a digital semaphone network which would be run by three operators and which would allow users to be contactable across Europe.
Belgium's first mobile service Proximus is run by Belgacom Mobile, 75-percent owned by Belgian state telephone operator Belgacom and 25-percent by AirTouch Communications Inc.
Belgacom is 49.9 percent owned by a consortium including U.S. Ameritech , Singapore Telecom and Tele Danmark and three Belgian investors, following its partial privatisation in December 1995.

Mobistar NV launched Belgium's second GSM network last August. Mobistar is 57 percent owned by France Telecom. Belgian data communications company Telinfo holds 10 percent and nine other Belgian companies the balance.
Belgium has more than half a million GSM users, with Proximus accounting for about 75 percent.
Mobistar has more than 120,000 customers. It expects to add at least another 100,000 clients by the end of this year.

Proximus is already profitable. Mobistar said last month it would stay deep in the red in 1997 but reach break-even by the turn of the century. It had a 1996 loss of 4.19 billion francs ($118 million) which was in line with expectations and caused by start-up costs.
Di Rupo said that the future operator of the third GSM network in Belgium will have to pay about nine billion francs ($255 million) for a licence to the Belgian state.
"The price of the third licence will be comparable to the one paid by the two existing operators," he said.
Since the third network would use the DCS 1800 technology, which requires more investment in antennae than is the case for existing GSM technology the amount might be revised down, he added.
Belgacom, however, immediately said it would oppose any discount that might be given a third operator.
"If it has always been said 'nine billion francs for everyone', then a discount is indeed not obvious," Belgacom spokesman Jan Margot told Reuters.
Margot said he did not see why the third operator would have more investment costs. "In a way they should have less costs since equipment becomes cheaper all the time," he said.

"The first two operators have also invested heavily to prepare the market, they have been about the biggest investors in advertising to make the GSM phenomenon known. The third operator benefits without having to invest or at least not that much," he added.

Eric Van Heesvelde, managing director of the Belgian Institute for Postal and Telecommunications Services (BIPT) which assesses the bids, said the ultimate goal was to ensure that none of the three operators would be dinumber of factors -- new licence conditions, investment costs, amounts paid by others -- and all elements combined should lead to an honest decision, based on what the third candidate is prepared to pay," he said.
